Lone Wolf BY GRAHAM EDWARDS he world was once much colder than it is now. The most recent glacial period in Earth's history - popularly known as the Ice Age - endured for roughly 100,000 years and ended perhaps 10,000 years ago. Throughout this deep-frozen age, early humans struggled to survive in harsh environments very different to those of today. Director Albert Hughes chose Ice Age Europe as the backdrop for his first solo feature outing, having collaborated with his brother, Allen, on films including From Hell and The Book of Eli. The story he conceived concerns a young hunter called Keda (Kodi Smit-McPhee) who becomes separated from his tribe. Befriending an injured wolf, Alpha, the boy develops such a powerful bond with the animal that Alpha evolves ultimately into the world's first dog. Screenwriter Daniele Sebastian Wiedenhaupt developed Hughes' tale of survival and friendship into a script entitled The Solutrean, the name referring to a group of Upper Paleolithic people who lived in Europe some 20,000 years ago. During production, the film was retitled Alpha. Tasked with re-creating the Ice Age world of Alpha, production visual effects super1 / 27 visor Jeffrey A. Okun worked with visual effects producer Denise Davis and production

manager Nicole Montemayor to place actors into frozen landscapes and bring them face ALPHA to face with extinct animals ranging from woolly mammoths to cave lions. The first meeting I had was with Albert Hughes and the producer, Andrew Rona," said Okun. "It was a really unique job interview because I didn't say a word - they essentially pitched the movie to me visually, talking about European sensibility and a lot of wide, graphic landscape shots. Then Albert went into vast scientific detail about what the Ice Age was and who the Solutreans were.i MPC, DNEG and Pixomondo took on the most complex visual effects assignments, with additional work done by CosFX, Flash Film Works, FreeStyle VFX, Rising Sun Pictures, Instinctual and RVX. Legend performed stereo conversion and also handled additional visual effects. With historical research a high priority, the production hired Dr. Jill Cook of The British Museum's Department of Britain, Europe and Prehistory as an archeological consultant. "The last Ice Age had warm and cold periods," explained Cook, "and 20,000 years ago was one of the deeply cold periods. Human life in Europe almost became extinct because the going got so tough - we were just hanging on by our fingernails. Cook's notes on Ice Age life turned a few preconceptions on their heads. 'The ice cover on the sea meant that there was less water in the atmosphere," she explained, iso there was less precipitation. So, while it was intensely cold and dry, and white with frost, this thought that people were constantly trudging through vast piles of snow is mythology. Also, when you see films about the deep past, the human characters are often dressed in unstitched bits of skins, and they're uncouth and savage. In fact, they had the 2 / 27 same mental capacities as we have. So here was a lovely chance to look at them as peo-

ple instead of something out of a comic book - a great opportunity to counteract all those myths.i Cook worked with costume designer Sharen Davis to align the film's wardrobe with current ideas about 20,000-year-old fashion, based both on evidence from ancient burials and on present-day practices in comparable cultures. "Arctic peoples today really value wolverine fur because the structure of the individual hairs is snow-repellent," Cook observed. 'They use it around their hoods and on their cuffs because it doesn't freeze to your skin, and so you don't get frostbite. Often these furs are used very decoratively, because hunting and killing a wolverine is no mean feat." Cook also introduced the filmmakers to Karl Lee of Primitive Technology UK, a professional in the art of making stone tools - known as knapping. They got big piles of flint for us and I advised Karl on the appropriate types of tools to make. He also taught the actors knapping so that when they were making their tools and weapons it looked authentic." effects team increased haze levels a little during postproduction. ¿As we started to put shots together," Jeffrey A. Okun said, "it was very difficult to sell distance and scope because everything was so clean. Everything looked like a matte painting. In the end, Albert stepped back a little bit from the no-atmosphere thing." Visual effects helped to polish another facet of Albert Hughes' approach - namely, ALPHA s part of his drive for historical accuracy, Hughes suggested that Ice Age skies should be free from dust and vapor, with distant horizons appearing crisp and sharp. While much of the film was photographed with this in mind, the visual 3 / 27

"Our camera operators were really good," remarked Okun, "but Albert got so frustrated because they would not lock the camera - they would always do minute little adjustments. Our visual effects editor, Neil Greenberg, would spend every night stabilizing every shot in the scene that they were working on in the edit. Some of the shots ended up as visual effects because when you stabilize a perspective move it tends to look Alfred Hitchcock-y. One shot got so loopy we decided to make the background CG, then we made the foreground CG. Then it was like, 'The wolf's in it so let's make that CG.' In the end, the only thing that wasn't CG was the sky!" Working with Hughes on the director's first foray into 3D filmmaking, production stereo supervisor Marcus Alexander recognized that the film's lingering landscape shots would give audiences ample opportunity to study the frame. "It wasn't about making everything super-deep," said Alexander. "It was about knowing we had the time to let the viewers' eyes roam and really look into the detail. This wasn't a flash-bang gimmicky movie where shots are eight frames long, and while you do as much as possible to suggest volume and depth you re never really going to register how clean a shot is. We had to make sure we didn't overly miniaturize things, or end up being overly divergent so that over that time your eyes start to hurt trying to look at that distant background. The way I sold it to Legend was to treat this like a National Geographic filmi Alexander began by compiling a depth script for the entire film, based on a 2D Avid cut. "I plotted out the overall interaxial distance, the overall disparity," he stated. "Then I 4 / 27 re-created that on a graph to end up with pixel depths based on the resolution of the

image, positive through negative, and also individual notes on how much volume I wanted, and where to plot and place everything." scoping to enhance details in the fur clothing of the hunters and the pelt of the wolf, Alpha. "We avoided doing the usual haircuts that you end up with post conversion," Alexander continued. "Often you shave off the flyaways in order to get an easy edge and avoid having to repaint behind. The intent on this movie was to capture each hair, place it back in depth and make sure it parallaxed correctly with the lens or with the movement of the object it was on. It was everything considered the worst nightmare for a post-conversion company to do!" Dash we shot a bue Angeles backlot hosted reshoots in the fall of 2017. A brief shoot in Iceland allowed the filmmakers to plant performers directly into subarctic terrain.iWe had two helicopters and a safety team in Iceland," Jeffrey A. Okun related. "We'd drop the safety team on various glaciers and they'd go scout it out. Then we'd drop our actor and our dog, and the safety guys would lie down dressed to look like snow blocks. The actor would walk 10 feet and then the helicopter would swoop in and pick them up. There's something to be said for shooting for real. It impacts the camerawork, the actors - it's visceral ALPHA Artists at Legend crafted 3D effects right down to the micro level, using intricate rotorincipal photography for Alpha took place in the spring and summer of 2016, during a six-week shoot on a bluescreen-backed lot in Burnaby, Vancouver, and on location in forests around the city and on the Siksika Nation reserve in Alberta. 'We shot in late winter when everything was covered in snow, and we shot again in summer. Iceland in the summer is pretty much bright 24 hours a day, and in the winter it's quite dark, so it was about logistically trying to figure out when we could fly the helicopters and get the times of day in the different spots. In addition, Einarsson's team used photogrammetry to re-create the Icelandic locations as Autodesk Maya models for use by other vendors. For this, the helicopter traversed the same stretches of landscape at three different heights. Photographers used two Sony a7R DSLR cameras - one at each side window - to capture up to 4,000 overlapping photographs at 7K resolution. The photographs then passed to Olafur Haraldsson, founder of photogrammetry specialists Designing Reality. There are many software options in the market," observed RVX CG supervisor Matthías Bjarnason, "but the reason we work with Olafur is that his software is designed to handle massive datasets. This wasn't just photogrammetry of a single asset like a rock or a tree. The area we covered was quite vast - a couple of kilometers in each direction. "For each photograph taken," Daöi Einarsson elaborated, "Olafur would give us a Maya camera with that photograph attached to it as an image plane. Matthias and his team would take that into The Foundry's MARI or Nuke to get the 3D meshed geometry textured. The mammoth was one of our old assets - it's been around here forever," noted MPC CG supervisor David Hirst. iWe upgraded it considerably, not only into the pipeline but also visually. We have such an extensive assets library now, and that helped with our efficiencies, especially when some of these creatures were only seen in a couple of shots. "We made another version that was just literally bones. Albert was very specific as to the position so we designed a 3D model in Pixologic ZBrush - that allowed us to change it and move it around. Once we got the design that he wanted, we taped out the shape on the floor and had a person stand next to it for scale. Then we printed a small version at maybe 1/16th scale for final approvali Sculptors fashioned some parts of the mammoth skeletons from foam; other sections were 3D-printed. The team coated the bones with fiberglass then added layers of ALPHA uring the opening act of Alpha, a group of hunters that includes Keda and his father, Tau (Jóhannes Haukur Jóhannesson), trek through a vast, frozen wilderness in search of food. Visual effects combined foregrounds shot in North Amer7 / 27

dried flesh and skin. "For the fleshy bits we used silicone," Jones commented. "We ran ALPHA the skin and made it look like it was collapsed and leathery. Other areas were just a fiberglass shell covered with hair. We had to truck it up to Canada so we broke the main body into three sections. The legs and the tusks were separate. For another sequence, KNB constructed a mechanical giant boar, again beginning with a digital model and progressing to a full-scale foam sculpture. Molds yielded a foamlatex skin, which enclosed an internal mechanical armature. The team covered the boar's body with synthetic fur fabric from National Fiber Technology, and used a transfer process to glue fur fibers to the face. Whiskers around the eyes and muzzle were handpunched. KNB artist Grady Holder custom-made acrylic eyes and tusks. On set, Carey Jones and makeup effects artist Mike Fields puppeteered the boar using durable cable controls. "It was in the throes of death," remarked Jones, "so we went pretty heavy-duty to give it all the hard motions that Albert wanted, and to alleviate any issues with mechanisms or cables snapping. Equally robust was the boar's breathing system, which relied on mechanics rather than easily-popped latex bladders. '¿We mounted a fiberglass shell to a steel mechanism with pistons, attached to a cable. The mechanism pushed the shell up and down and motivated the foam latex skin. A flexible tube extended from off-camera up the boar's backside and through its body, enabling a crewmember to deliver spurts of vapor from between the beast's jaws. As the hunters journey on, a one-minute time-lapse shot tracks their progress over the course of five days and four nights. Beginning with a live-action plate of the group, 8 / 27 the shot transitions into an eagle's-eye view that speeds through the landscape while

ALPHA the sun and stars wheel around the heavens. Eventually the camera decelerates into a cave, where the shot ends on a second plate of the hunters at rest inside. "Albert was very particular about how the camera moved," Jeffrey A. Okun recalled, "because this is one of the few times in the film that the camera does move. We started off with a game engine and helicopter hand control, and Albert flew the camera through simulated landscapes. It was really weird for me because my life is based in physics, and physics was not what Albert wanted - he wanted these severe turns but with a level horizon. We came up with a term that we used a lot on this movie: 'liquid reality.' Slowly I snuck in a little bit of banking here and there so it became more of a rollercoaster ride. Pixomondo spent roughly four months crafting the time-lapse shot, first developing previs then constructing a vast digital landscape based on the Iceland reference.iWe created our landscapes based off the photos, using photogrammetry intenselyi explained Pixomondo visual effects supervisor Boris Schmidt. They didn't want snow in the scene, but a lot of the photos had tons of snow in them; so we used textures from other areas and painted it out." Utilizing Agisoft Photoscan software, the team replicated specific landmarks such as the dramatic Háifoss waterfall. "Of course, the photogrammetry gave us a static waterfall. We painted out the water and projected footage of waterfalls onto simple card geometriesi Extending its horizons beyond the Iceland reference, the team incorporated terrain generated procedurally from height fields using World Machine software. Millions of scattered rocks and pebbles added texture. The complete landscape came together as a single 9 / 27 gigantic asset in Autodesk 3ds Max.

Albert is a very studied transition guy - as am I, based on my upbringing with Saul Bass," remarked Jeffrey A. Okun. "In this film we do a lot of what I call 'weighted dissolves,' where the uninteresting parts fade out first and you're left for a beat with, say, the main character's eyeball matching up to the sun. Things line up. FreeStyle VFX worked on weighted transitions in which dancing embers from a campfire linger across the dissolve and survive into the subsequent shot. ¿The production shot some live-action elementsi said FreeStyle visual effects supervisor Eran Barnea. "But we mostly used particle systems and then composited them into the live-action plates. We had to match the director's vision - the embers were moving much slower than they would in reality - so in order to have full control we had to do it in 3D. Many times he wanted to use them out of focus, to have this magical effect. It's stylized, but still realistici FreeStyle also delivered day-for-night shots, and performed cosmetic fixes to enhance grimy character makeup. The stereo team carefully controlled the positions of the embers in 3D space to carry the viewers' eyes comfortably across the dissolves. Knowing that the director would be experimenting with transition timing in the digital intermediate, artists mocked up stereo effects over length, providing extra frames at the beginning and end of each shot. "Dissolves can sometimes be pretty ugly in stereo," remarked Marcus Alexander, "because you have different convergences between the A- and B-sides. We would make sure the embers were in the right depth on the A-side, maybe animate the depth to make the most I1 / 27 of the stereo during the transition, then animate back to where they should be located

in the B-side. We baked all that in so that when they rebuilt it in the DI, it made sense." For another transition, Rising Sun Pictures contributed a view of a sunrise seen from the cave entrance. Neil Greenberg provided a layout showing a flock of starlings describing fluid murmuration patterns in the dawn sky, animated in Adobe After Effects. Artists at RSP stitched live-action plates into a digital matte painting of the environment and recreated the flock of birds using Houdini. "It was a tiny piece of work that we did on the film," said RSP managing director Tony Clark, who acted as the company's visual effects supervisor on the project. "I knew nobody else here had time to supervise anything, so that's why I got it! It was really nice. I got to sit on the floor with a crew of about three artists, and we just chipped away at it." deaths. The hunters then harvest the bodies for meat and fur. The filmmakers had originally planned to shoot live-action for much of the hunt, but visual effects gradually took over as the edit evolved. All the bison visible in the final sequence are digital animals created by DNEG. DNEG visual effects supervisor Neil Eskuri attended a weeklong live-action shoot on an Alberta bison ranch. Professional wranglers directed the thunderous bovine action, which the crew photographed using drones and a Ford Raptor 4x4 with an onboard crane arm. "We set up scenes very similar to the storyboards," related Eskuri. "It was the best ALPHA eda and his companions locate their prey - a herd of several hundred bison. The hunters exploit a historically documented strategy known as a 'buffalo jump,' stampeding the beasts over a cliff edge and causing them to fall to their 12 / 27

ALPHA reference that animation would ever have. Bison are remarkably agile for creatures that weigh 2,000 pounds, and all of our animators were impressed with how quickly they could move. Something like 65 percent of their body weight is in their shoulders and over their front legs - they kind of use their back legs to steer. The bison of Alpha closely resemble the modern North American bison, with horns enlarged to suggest a more ancient species. For DNEG CG supervisor Alesandro Ongaro and his team, one ranch animal in particular provided the perfect model. "This bison's name was Stan," said Eskuri. "Everything we did was based off Stan, and then we made variations on the size, color, horns and groom. We ended up with 30-35 different animals, although with bison they all pretty much look the same!" Photographs captured Stan in all his glory - even venturing inside his mouth and nostrils - and enabled artists to construct a master bison asset from which to spawn the rest of the herd. "We broke off the work into two prongs," Eskuri explained. "One dealt with the fur and the other with the musculature. Fortunately for us, bison are pretty much covered in fur, so we weren't really going to see a lot of muscle flex. Remi Cauzid, our creature TD, used rudimentary muscles for the large bits, giving the muscles volume and allowing skin sliding, then localized clusters and shapes on top. Those were automated, so if the foot came down with a hard jolt, that force would be percolated through to the clusters. When the director wanted more jiggle or bulge in certain areas, animation had tools to adjust those clusters rather than trying to deal with it through a full muscle system. It was very localized control. 13 / 27 More challenging was the fur, which required grooming lead Dameon Oboyle to repli-

ALPHA cate a six-inch-thick pelt that ran the gamut from curly to straight, wavy to tightly-napped. "Bison fur is ridiculously thick," commented Eskuri, "and when they turn, it compresses and then opens up. We started with the basic bison model, then put a sort of shell on top of that to give us an overall volume of fur. Not only could the groomers use that but also animation, so once the bison were bumping and jostling one another in the herd, the animators would know where the fur was going to intersect." Different render layers added dirt and dangling straggles of grass and straw. Effects simulations surrounded the beasts with buzzing insects and floating dust tufts. Animation supervisor Aaron Gilman used keyframe animation to replicate the behavior of the real bison, and employed DNEG's proprietary Maya-based crowd system to manage a herd of around 275 animals. To ease the rendering load caused by the complex fur dynamics, the team divided the herd into groups of around 25 individuals. Breaking it up made it more efficient," said Eskuri. "We would run the simulation and find one or two bison that were doing the wrong thing. Then we could go into our crowd simulation and change their performance, or just pluck them out completely. We could turn around a full crowd simulation in a day." Production shot live-action of the hunters on open plains at the Siksika Nation reserve. DNEG expanded the plates into a 3D Ice Age environment, based on photogrammetry of the location and on production concept art. Norway's 2,000-foot-high Preikestolen Rock, also known as Preacher's Pulpit, provided the template for the deadly cliff. "We took the concept art and started laying in big chunks of geometry to give the 14 / 27 director the overall scope," Eskuri explained. "Once we got the layout in place, we would

move the camera around to match Albert's storyboards or, in a few cases, come up with interesting shots that we gave to him. Everything you see is 3D, but with most of the big shots we knew where the camera was going to be so we just did digital matte paintings and projected those onto the geometry based on the camera position. We didn't texture everything because it was just too massive. Artists rotoscoped the hunters out of the live-action plates, projected them onto cards and placed them into the digital environment among the CG bison. Using similar techniques, DNEG augmented Ice Age environments seen elsewhere in the film, including in scenes of the tribe's home village. cliff edge. Albert Hughes marked this turning point in the hunt with an uncharacteristically dynamic fully digital shot in which the camera arcs alongside the weapons as they fly through the air. "Because we were doing all new animation in post," Eskuri commented, it opened the director up to put in shots that he hadn't really thought of before. The 'spear's eye view' was one of those. For shots of the bison plummeting over the cliff edge, animators tracked down documentary footage of falling bison and sheep, and studied the 2005 DreamWorks miniseries Into the West, which re-enacted a Lakota buffalo jump. The team paid close attention to the laws of physics, ensuring the huge animals maintained the correct momentum and taking into account their front-heavy weight distribution. Still, the scant video referALPHA critical moment during the stampede has the hunters hurling their spears at the onrushing bison. The weapons fall short and plant themselves in a quivering line - a blocking tactic that panics the herd back towards the waiting 15 / 27

ALPHA ence raised more questions than it answered. Are the legs still kicking when they go over?" questioned Eskuri. "Are they tumbling? Are they screaming? I believe that if any creature goes over a 200-foot cliff, there's a moment of panic and then their whole body just shuts down. So that's what we did. As they go over there's a little bit of motion with the legs or head, and a little scream. Then they just became like rocks falling through the air." At the height of the action, a charging bison snags Keda in its horns and tosses him over the cliff. Second unit director and stunt coordinator Robert Alonzo attached Kodi Smit-McPhee or his stunt double to a blue-painted buck mounted on a 4x4 vehicle traveling at around 25 miles per hour. A crane-mounted wire rig flipped a stunt performer for a pivotal slow-motion shot of Keda flying through the air. DNEG refined critical poses with computer generated limbs, replaced the truck with a digital bison and introduced a digi-double Keda for medium and wide shots. heda lands unconscious on a ledge halfway down the cliff face. Unable to either rouse or reach their companion, the other hunters descend to harvest the bison meat. Eventually, they depart, believing the unresponsive Keda to be dead. The art department built sets representing different sections of the cliff, including the upper edge from which the tribal hunters attempt to reach Keda and the ledge on which the youngster is stranded. DNEG extended the cliff laterally and vertically, and created a 200-foot-tall edifice based on the Preikestolen reference. Keda wakes to find a vulture pecking at his face, whereupon he seizes the bird and 16 / 27 wrings its neck. KNB manufactured a dummy bird based on an African white-backed vul-

ALPHA ture provided as a living, breathing reference by Los Angeles-based Birds and Animals Unlimited.iMark Forbes, the animal trainer, brought the real vulture into the shop, which was terrifying!" recalled Carey Jones. "It looked at you like you were food! We took pictures, measured it and sent a sculpture to Albert for approval, and to Mark so that he could give us his notes. Then we fabricated the body and individually hand-attached all the feathers to the wings. For the neck-breaking part, we came up with a simple mechanism that was stiff, and then the moment Kodi twisted its neck it went limp. We did that with a series of cables and magnetsi MPC replaced the practical vulture with a CG bird. Compositors locked the actor to the digital vulture using 2D warps and elements lifted from separate takes.iIn one shot we used the feet of KNB's dummy," said MPC 2D supervisor Nick Whiteley. "It was standing on his chest and we were spending all this time trying to get our CG feet to depress his clothes properly. The practical feet looked great so we added a bit of color correct and made a join with the CG." A storm builds and rain pours down, causing a flash flood that fills the canyon below the cliffs with muddy water. Seizing this perilous opportunity to escape, Keda leaps from the ledge into the torrent. DNEG enhanced its cliff extensions with a variety of extreme weather effects. Working in Houdini, effects lead Gero Grimm simulated debris-filled water inspired by video of Arizona flash floods. During his fight for survival, Keda breaks his ankle. KNB presented concepts for prosthetic injury makeup, but struggled initially to match the director's vision. "Eventu17 / 27 ally, Albert told me this story of when he fractured his ankle," Carey Jones related. "He

gave me this grotesque description of how his whole foot was swollen and bruised. Based upon what he said, we matched the final look to that.i Mike Fields applied silicone prosthetics to Kodi Smit-McPhee's ankle. For an insert shot in which Keda wedges his ankle between rocks and wrenches the joint back into place, KNB manufactured an articulated dummy limb from a cast of the actor's leg. their injuries, a bond begins to grow between boy and wolf.iAt around the same time as we were making the film," said Jill Cook, "we started getting archeological evidence from Russia and genetic evidence from work being done in the U.S. that the domestication of the dog actually had taken place at about the period in which this film was set. Impossible Journey BY JOE FORDHAM an the 1960s, opponents of the United States space program cited the mythological character of Icarus, who stole his father's wax-and-feather wings and soared too close to the sun, as a symbol of hubris. The 'space race,' critics maintained, was a reckless reaction to the launch of the Soviet Union satellite, Sputnik 1. But President Kennedy's 1962 speech, which challenged Americans to place an astronaut on the moon by the decade's end, went on to inspire an unprecedented feat of courage and engineering hutzpah. Historian James Hansen's 654-page biography, First Man: The Life of Neil Armstrong, traced the journey to the moon from the perspective of Neil Alden Armstrong, a young aviator from Ohio who fulfilled Kennedy's challenge. The story captured the imagination of filmmaker Damien Chazelle, director of 2016's La La Land. "Having grown up with the moon landing in the rear view," said Chazelle, "it felt like an event that later generations take for granted. People don't ask too many questions about what it might have meant, and what it took to accomplish. I became fascinated with the idea of trying to tackle this huge event of global significance, but from an intimate, subjective point of 1/31 view. I wanted to look at the years leading up to the moon landing, to show step-by-step

FIRST MAN how that became a reality, and I wanted to locate that almost exclusively from the perspective of Neil Armstrong, his wife and his family, to show what that cost them." Screenwriter Josh Singer focused on eight critical years leading to NASA's Apollo 11 moonshot, manned by commander Armstrong (Ryan Gosling), lunar module pilot Buzz Aldrin (Corey Stoll) and command module pilot Mike Collins (Lukas Haas). The narrative charted personal details in the lives of Armstrong and his wife Janet (Claire Foy), including the death of their infant daughter Karen (Lucy Stafford), Neil's training with the X-15 rocket-powered jet, the Gemini 8 Earth-orbit rendezvous, and his eventual, historic landing on the moon's Sea of Tranquility, July 20, 1969. Chazelle laid out shooting plans in an animatic reel that he compiled with film editor Tom Cross. "We had a script and a breakdown from the studio," recalled visual effects producer Kevin Elam. "As we got into budgeting, Damien came in with his animatic. He had storyboarded almost every sequence that involved visual effects, and cut that to music. And he handed out a 300-page document describing how he was going to make the movie. He was extraordinarily well prepared." NASA offered its assistance with archival reference and location facilities. We had complete access," commented production designer Nathan Crowley. "We were allowed access to the astronaut's homes in El Lago, Florida. We filmed the crawler that carried the Saturn V rocket to its launch pad, and we shot in the vehicle assembly building. Intrigued, he began traveling the 70-plus miles from Los Angeles to the Inland Empire to attend motocross events, meeting the participants and listening to their stories. iI was amazed to discover this incredible community and youth culture that revolved around riding dirt bikes in these vast spaces," said Daly. "I thought it would be a beautiful way to do a science fiction story, to set it in this real world that was also very fast, very neon, with these bikes flying through the air." While immersing himself in the motocross world, Daly also wrote down story ideas as they came to him, and created one iteration after another of the Artificial Intelligence dog — ultimately named A.X.L. for 'Attack, Exploration and Logistics.' "As I put things together," Daly said, "I started to see that the best way to get this movie made was with a proof-of-concept short. So we raised money on Kickstarter, and I shot three days out in the desert in the Inland Empire."
